title: Advances in the management of intraocular foreign bodies
study_design: Mini review of published literature on the management of intraocular foreign bodies (IOFBs).

population.description: People with ocular trauma involving intraocular foreign bodies (IOFBs); the review does not define a recruited cohort.

condition_or_topic: Management of intraocular foreign bodies (IOFBs) after ocular trauma
clinical_background: IOFBs are a serious complication of ocular trauma that can cause substantial visual morbidity and present difficult management decisions. Published estimates indicate that IOFBs occur in 18-41% of open globe injuries. Their location and composition affect surgical planning and urgency: most are found in the posterior segment, iron and copper can cause ocular toxicity, and organic material carries an increased risk of endophthalmitis. Reported estimates of endophthalmitis risk with retained IOFBs range from 5% to 30%. The optimal timing of removal remains debated, while final visual acuity varies.
objectives: Review current clinical practices, disputed aspects of care, and advances in IOFB management.
Describe a systematic approach to preoperative assessment and surgical management, particularly removal of posterior-segment IOFBs by pars plana vitrectomy.
Examine the advantages, disadvantages, and published evidence concerning immediate versus delayed removal, and synthesize the literature to guide surgical care and patient outcomes.
main_conclusion: The authors conclude that management of intraocular foreign bodies (IOFBs) requires careful examination, orbital CT without contrast for localization, and globe closure before extraction. Removal may be immediate or delayed according to the patient’s condition, visibility, and clinical setting; pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) remains the principal approach for posterior-segment IOFBs, while further research is needed to clarify complications, visual prognostic factors, and optimal surgery.
narrative_summary:
This mini review synthesizes published evidence on the frequency, assessment, treatment, and outcomes of intraocular foreign bodies (IOFBs). IOFBs are estimated to occur in 18-41% of open globe injuries, and occupational exposure accounts for many cases. The authors emphasize a thorough but gentle examination, including slit-lamp biomicroscopy and assessment of the posterior segment. Orbital CT without contrast is the preferred initial imaging study when an IOFB is suspected; it can identify an IOFB in up to 95% of patients. Magnetic resonance imaging is contraindicated if a metallic foreign body is suspected.

Initial management prioritizes globe closure. The timing of extraction depends on the patient’s stability, the foreign body’s composition, the injury, visualization, and surgical resources. Toxic metals and organic material call for immediate removal; signs of endophthalmitis also indicate immediate surgery unless a simultaneous life-threatening injury precludes it. Delayed extraction may be appropriate in other circumstances. For posterior-segment IOFBs, PPV is the main surgical approach. The review also discusses antimicrobial prophylaxis and techniques for removing difficult-to-grasp objects.

Visual prognosis varies: published reports indicate that at least 21% of affected eyes have final visual acuity worse than 20/200. The authors recommend counseling on eye protection and, when outcomes are poor, monocular precautions and low-vision support. They also stress assessment for trauma-related mental health conditions.
interpretation: Management of intraocular foreign bodies (IOFBs) depends on the patient's condition, the foreign body's location and composition, and whether it can be visualized and removed safely. Closing the globe is the initial surgical priority; removal and repair of additional intraocular damage may follow if they cannot be completed safely during the same operation. Removal may be immediate or delayed according to the clinical circumstances, while pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) is the principal approach for posterior-segment IOFBs. Final visual outcomes vary, and the Ocular Trauma Score can help estimate prognosis.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The literature reviewed does not establish one removal schedule for every injury. Evidence discussed by the authors suggests that immediate removal may reduce endophthalmitis and proliferative vitreoretinopathy, but it has not been associated with significant visual improvement. A retrospective study by Chaudhry et al. associated a delay of over 48 hours in globe repair and IOFB removal with greater endophthalmitis risk and poorer vision. By contrast, a military series of 79 eyes reported no endophthalmitis despite removal an average of 21 days after injury; almost all patients (97%) received systemic (86%) and/or topical (85%) antibiotics. The authors caution that all IOFBs in that series resulted from exploding ordnance, whose heat may have reduced contamination. Prior comparisons also associated external electromagnet extraction, rather than PPV, with significantly worse functional and anatomical outcomes and higher rates of endophthalmitis, vitreous hemorrhage, and proliferative vitreoretinopathy.
clinical_implications: The risk of endophthalmitis and the urgency of extraction differ by IOFB composition; organic material and toxic metals call for immediate removal, whereas inert material may remain longer with fewer complications.

Delaying extraction can allow corneal edema and intraocular inflammation to subside, potentially improving surgical visualization, but the suitability of delay depends on the injury and the patient's condition.
Zone of Injury and Ocular Trauma Score can inform visual prognostication and early counseling. Zone 3 injury and more severe injury are associated with the worst visual prognosis.
At least 21% of eyes with IOFBs have final visual acuity worse than 20/200. Patients with poor visual outcomes may need support for monocular vision and adaptation to their remaining sight.
Traumatic ocular injury can have mental-health consequences; the cited small pediatric cohort reported anxiety-related disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, and depression in 15% of patients.
practice_implications: Encourage eye protection during work and other high-risk exposures, and counsel patients with prior IOFB injury about protecting their eyes around chemicals, lasers, metal, and UV equipment.

Assess suspected IOFB carefully with visual acuity and pupillary examination, slit lamp biomicroscopy, and examination of the posterior segment, including indirect ophthalmoscopy. Avoid measuring intraocular pressure or otherwise pressing on a potentially open globe before wound closure.
Use orbital CT without contrast as first-line imaging when an IOFB is suspected and its location is needed for surgical planning. Do not use MRI when a metallic foreign body is suspected.

Initially protect the affected eye with a shield, provide intramuscular tetanus toxoid prophylaxis, control nausea and pain as needed, and consider broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics to prevent endophthalmitis.

Prioritize globe closure before attempting IOFB extraction. Choose the timing of removal according to physiologic stability, foreign-body composition, injury characteristics, visibility, care setting, and availability of trained personnel. Remove the IOFB immediately when endophthalmitis is evident unless a simultaneous life-threatening injury prevents surgery; delay removal when the patient is hemodynamically unstable.

Remove toxic metals such as iron and copper, and organic foreign bodies, immediately. Use an approach tailored to the IOFB's location, size, and composition; PPV is the mainstay for posterior-segment IOFBs.
After extraction, examine the peripheral retina, treat retinal breaks, and consider tamponade as indicated. The routine use of a prophylactic scleral buckle remains debated.
For patients with poor visual outcomes, discuss continuous use of monocular precautions with 3 mm polycarbonate lenses and safety frames, and consider referral to a low-vision specialist.
Assess patients for mental-health difficulties related to the injury during postoperative care and refer those who may benefit from specialist support.
open_questions: What is the optimal timing and surgical approach for IOFB removal across differing clinical circumstances?
When does prophylactic scleral buckling benefit patients undergoing IOFB removal?
future_directions: Investigate the acute and chronic complications of IOFB injuries.
Clarify which factors improve final visual outcomes.
Determine the most suitable surgical approaches for patients with IOFBs.

main_findings.context: Estimate from studies cited in this literature review.

main_findings.context: Estimate from studies cited in this literature review.

main_findings.context: Range reported from cited literature on foreign body location.

main_findings.context: Range reported from cited literature on foreign body location.

main_findings.context: The source groups the lens and orbit together for this range.

main_findings.description: Most cited sources placed the overall risk of endophthalmitis among eyes with retained intraocular foreign bodies within this range.
main_findings.context: Estimate for all retained intraocular foreign bodies.

main_findings.description: Colyer et al. found this approximate frequency of endophthalmitis across the intraocular foreign body literature they reviewed.
main_findings.context: Average across literature from the past 30 years; this is a finding attributed to the cited review.

main_findings.description: The cited literature reported acute postoperative endophthalmitis after cataract surgery at this frequency.
main_findings.context: Presented as a comparison with endophthalmitis associated with retained intraocular foreign bodies.

main_findings.description: The cited literature reported acute postoperative endophthalmitis after pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) at this frequency.
main_findings.context: Presented as a comparison with endophthalmitis associated with retained intraocular foreign bodies.

main_findings.description: Chaudhry et al. associated later open globe repair and intraocular foreign body removal with greater endophthalmitis risk and poorer visual outcomes.
main_findings.context: Finding of a retrospective study published in 2008, not an analysis conducted by this review.

main_findings.description: Cited research identified early primary repair as an independent protective factor against endophthalmitis following open globe injuries.
main_findings.context: Intraocular tissue prolapse and self-sealing wounds were also reported as independent protective factors. Lens disruption and delayed primary wound closure were associated with higher endophthalmitis rates.

main_findings.description: Cited studies associated Zone 3 injuries, larger wounds, and retinal detachment with the poorest visual prognosis and the highest enucleation rates.
main_findings.context: These are associations reported in prior studies, not comparative results generated by this review.

main_findings.description: A clinical eye examination may fail to identify an intraocular foreign body in this proportion of patients.
main_findings.context: Diagnostic finding attributed to cited research.

main_findings.description: Orbital computed tomography without contrast can detect intraocular foreign bodies in this proportion of patients.
main_findings.context: Detection estimate from cited research; manual measurements of foreign body dimensions on these scans were reported to be inconsistent and often inaccurate.

main_findings.description: Gentle B-scan ultrasonography can identify posterior-segment foreign bodies in this proportion of patients with intraocular foreign bodies.
main_findings.context: Estimate from cited research; the review notes operator dependence and the danger of applying pressure to an open globe.

main_findings.description: Cited research found that immediate foreign body removal may lower endophthalmitis and proliferative vitreoretinopathy risk compared with delayed removal, without an associated significant improvement in vision.
main_findings.context: Immediate removal means extraction during the same operation as globe closure. The review presents the potential risk reduction cautiously.

main_findings.description: A recent cited study reported postoperative endophthalmitis after combined globe repair and intraocular foreign body removal within the specified interval.
main_findings.context: Removal occurred within 24 hours of the initial injury.

main_findings.description: A cited study in military personnel reported no endophthalmitis after delayed removal of intraocular foreign bodies.
main_findings.context: The study included 79 eyes injured during Operation Iraqi Freedom and Operation Enduring Freedom; removal occurred an average of 21 days after initial injury. All foreign bodies resulted from exploding ordnance.

main_findings.description: Most patients in the cited military study received antibiotics while awaiting intraocular foreign body removal.
main_findings.context: Coverage was systemic (86%) and/or topical (85%) in the study of 79 eyes. The authors suggest delayed removal with adequate coverage may carry minimal endophthalmitis risk in combat ocular trauma.

main_findings.description: The review reports an association between combined vitreoretinal surgery using a temporary keratoprosthesis (TKP) and subsequent penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) failure.
main_findings.context: The association was noted particularly when silicone oil was used; no failure rate was supplied.

main_findings.description: Compared with PPV, external electromagnet removal was associated with significantly worse functional and anatomical outcomes in cited research.
main_findings.context: The electromagnet-treated eyes also had higher rates of endophthalmitis, vitreous hemorrhage, and proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR); comparative rates were not provided.

main_findings.description: Cited evidence suggests prophylactic scleral buckling may help prevent retinal detachment after removal of intraocular foreign bodies by PPV.
main_findings.context: The review describes routine prophylactic use as debated.

main_findings.description: A cited study associated prophylactic scleral buckling in posterior-segment open globe injuries with better final visual and anatomical outcomes and a non-significant reduction in subsequent retinal detachments.
main_findings.context: The decrease in retinal detachment must not be interpreted as statistically significant.

main_findings.description: The cited literature reports that at least this proportion of eyes with intraocular foreign bodies end with visual acuity worse than the stated threshold.
main_findings.metric: proportion with final visual acuity worse than 20/200
main_findings.context: The Ocular Trauma Score is described as a reliable predictor of final vision.

main_findings.description: Cited studies associated several presenting findings and injury characteristics with poorer visual prognosis after an intraocular foreign body.
main_findings.context: Reported factors were age greater than 50, worse initial visual acuity, hyphema, vitreous hemorrhage, uveal prolapse, retinal detachment, afferent pupillary defect, retinal hemorrhage, complications of retinal breaks, intraocular perfluoropropane (C3F8) gas tamponade, central corneal perforation, corneoscleral laceration, larger foreign bodies, and posterior-segment location. Higher postoperative PVR and phthisis bulbi rates were also associated with intraocular foreign bodies.

main_findings.description: Cited research associated specified features with better visual outcomes after intraocular foreign body injury.
main_findings.context: These features were better presenting visual acuity, no retinal breaks, no vitreous hemorrhage, wound length less than 4 mm, and non-vitrectomy surgery.

main_findings.description: A small cited pediatric cohort reported mental health disorders following ocular trauma at this frequency.
main_findings.context: The disorders reported were generalized anxiety disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, and depression; the review does not provide separate rates for each.

notable_adverse_events: Compared with PPV, external electromagnet removal was associated with higher endophthalmitis, vitreous hemorrhage, and PVR rates; numerical rates were not reported.
Combined vitreoretinal surgery with TKP was associated with subsequent PKP failure, particularly with silicone oil; no rate was reported.
A large pars plana incision can increase retinal incarceration, vitreous hemorrhage, and retinal detachment risk; no rates were reported.
The review describes a potential for subretinal PFCL migration when retinal tears or detachments are present; no rate was reported.
Some cited models suggest that a foreign body entering PFCL may descend more quickly toward the macula; no rate was reported.
Use of an intraocular magnet alone can allow a foreign body to detach during extraction, fall posteriorly, and injure the retina; no rate was reported.

scales_and_classifications.name: Zone of Injury (ZOI)
scales_and_classifications.description: Classifies open globe injuries by rupture location: Zone 1 covers the cornea and limbus, Zone 2 extends 5 mm posterior to the limbus, and Zone 3 lies beyond 5 mm; Zone 3a spans 5 to 8 mm and Zone 3b lies greater than 8 mm posterior to the limbus.

scales_and_classifications.name: Ocular Trauma Score (OTS)
scales_and_classifications.description: A tool for predicting final visual acuity after ocular injury using initial visual acuity, globe rupture, endophthalmitis, perforating injury, retinal detachment and relative afferent pupillary defect.

document_sections.heading: Advances in the management of intraocular foreign bodies
document_sections.content: This literature review examines current approaches, disputed decisions, and developments in the care of intraocular foreign bodies (IOFBs), a serious consequence of ocular trauma that can cause substantial morbidity. It describes a systematic approach to preoperative assessment and surgery that the authors say should be used for each case. Foreign-body location and composition affect operative technique and timing, particularly when toxic metals or vegetable material are involved. The review compares immediate with delayed extraction, emphasizes pars plana vitrectomy for posterior-segment IOFBs, and discusses the variable final visual acuity and its prediction with the Ocular Trauma Score. Its purpose is to help clinicians improve the likelihood of surgical success and favorable patient outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content:
Traumatic eye injury is an important cause of visual loss in the United States and elsewhere. Recent studies estimate approximately 4.5 open globe injuries (OGIs) per 100,000 population annually in the United States; IOFBs are estimated to accompany 18-41% of OGIs. Data from the 2019 Global Burden of Disease Study indicate that the global age-standardized incidence rate of IOFBs fell <1% between 1990 and 2019, although global incidence rose from around 350 cases per 100,000 in 2008 to over 450 cases per 100,000 in 2019. Incidence is highest in developing countries, where manufacturing and agricultural work—occupations with elevated ocular-injury risk—often employ a larger share of workers. According to the US Eye Injury Registry, IOFBs most often affect men aged 21 to 40 years old. Injuries frequently occur at work (54-72%) or at home (30%); hammers, power tools, and weapons or explosives are common mechanisms. Studies from Ireland, Greece, and China likewise describe a predominance of young men in manual work. Eye protection is often absent at the time of injury.

IOFBs can be categorized by material and site, although either characteristic may initially be uncertain or inferred. Identifying anterior versus posterior location and lens involvement informs surgical planning. The posterior segment contains most IOFBs (58%-88%); the anterior segment accounts for 10%-15%, and the lens or orbit for 2%-8%. Frequent metallic materials include iron, copper, lead, zinc, aluminum, and nickel. Iron can cause siderosis bulbi and copper can cause chalcosis. Glass, wood, concrete, and plastic are also described as inert foreign-body materials. Organic material, including vegetable matter, insects, and animal hair, presents a greater endophthalmitis risk than other IOFBs.

Most sources put the overall endophthalmitis risk with retained IOFBs between 5% and 30%. In literature from the past 30 years reviewed by Colyer et al., the average reported occurrence was about 6.5%. By comparison, reported acute postoperative endophthalmitis rates are around 0.1% after cataract surgery and 0.05% after pars plana vitrectomy (PPV). A 2008 retrospective study by Chaudhry et al. associated a delay of over 48 hours in OGI repair and IOFB removal with greater endophthalmitis risk and worse visual outcomes. Post-traumatic endophthalmitis often has a more severe course than endophthalmitis of other causes. Rural injuries have been linked to higher endophthalmitis rates, including B. cereus endophthalmitis. Crystalline-lens disruption and delayed primary wound closure have also been linked to higher rates. In a cited study of OGIs, early primary repair (within 24 hours), intraocular tissue prolapse, and self-sealing wounds independently protected against endophthalmitis.

Material and location influence whether prompt extraction is needed. Organic substances and toxic metals generally warrant immediate removal, whereas other materials may remain longer. Decisions about timing should account for foreign-body size, position, and composition; injury mechanism; and the surgical team's capabilities. For an initial globe injury with a known or suspected IOFB, the primary objective is globe closure for extraction. Removing the IOFB and repairing other intraocular abnormalities are important secondary goals. If poor visualization, such as corneal edema or media opacity, or the patient's overall condition in a polytrauma setting prevents safe completion at the initial operation, these goals may need to be addressed in the near future.

document_sections.heading: Management and preoperative planning
document_sections.content:
The Zone of Injury (ZOI) classifies OGIs by rupture location. Zone 1 covers the cornea and limbus; Zone 2 extends through the 5 mm posterior to the limbus; and Zone 3 includes the globe beyond 5 mm posterior to the limbus. Zone 3a is 5 to 8 mm posterior to the limbus, whereas Zone 3b is greater than 8 mm posterior to it. Zone 3 injuries and more severe injuries, including larger wounds and retinal detachment, have been associated with the poorest visual prognosis and the highest enucleation rates. Kuhn et al. proposed the Ocular Trauma Score (OTS) to predict final visual acuity after ocular injury. Its variables are presenting visual acuity, globe rupture, endophthalmitis, perforating injury, retinal detachment, and relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). The presence of any listed adverse variable, or poorer initial visual acuity, predicts a less favorable final acuity. Establishing ZOI and OTS before surgery may assist prognosis and early counseling about expected outcomes.

For suspected IOFB, initial assessment includes visual acuity, afferent pupillary defects, pupil size and shape, and inspection of the eyelids and eyebrows for external foreign bodies. Careful slit-lamp biomicroscopy is essential. Scleral or corneal laceration, a positive Seidel test, and uveal prolapse confirm an OGI and may raise suspicion of an IOFB. Iris transillumination defects can indicate an otherwise occult rupture and IOFB. An identified entry site may help locate the foreign body. Thorough posterior-segment examination is important because most IOFBs are found there. Occult IOFBs may instead become apparent through later intraocular inflammation, sometimes granulomatous in appearance. As with other possible OGIs, intraocular-pressure measurement and examination maneuvers that press on the globe should generally wait until wound closure, to avoid further intraocular injury or extrusion of ocular contents. Some advocate postponing pharmacologic mydriasis when the iris has prolapsed, because dilation might reopen the defect. When blast injury or military shrapnel is involved, the fellow eye also needs careful evaluation for occult trauma, alongside treatment of simultaneous life-threatening injuries. The article includes an IOFB-management and decision-making algorithm.

Localization guides treatment and operative planning. Lens opacity, corneal injury, hyphema, or vitreous hemorrhage can obscure an IOFB, and clinical eye examination may miss it in up to 55% of patients. Orbital X-ray has been used for metallic IOFBs but is limited for radiolucent materials; computed tomography (CT) has consequently replaced it as the preferred imaging test when an IOFB is suspected. Noncontrast orbital CT identifies IOFBs in up to 95% of patients. A CT limitation is that manual measurements of foreign-body dimensions on scans can be inconsistent and often inaccurate. Gentle B-scan ultrasonography can detect posterior-segment foreign bodies in up to 52% of patients with IOFBs, but demands extreme caution. It may be particularly helpful during surgery for a foreign body settled anteriorly in the pars plana and difficult to see directly. B-scan findings depend on the operator, and excessive probe pressure risks expelling intraocular contents. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may detect organic matter but is contraindicated when a metallic foreign body is suspected, because movement of the object could further damage the eye.

Initial care includes an eye shield, intramuscular tetanus toxoid prophylaxis (0.5 mL), antiemetics when needed, adequate analgesia, and consideration of broad-spectrum intravenous (IV) antibiotics to prevent endophthalmitis. Patients typically begin IV antibiotics immediately after diagnosis and change to oral medication at discharge to finish treatment. Overall antibiotic duration varies, but typically ranges from 48 hours to 7-10 days. Given IV or orally, levofloxacin and moxifloxacin have achieved aqueous and vitreous concentrations sufficient to inhibit 90% of major ocular pathogen isolates (MIC90), making them popular prophylactic choices. Typical IV or oral doses are levofloxacin 500 mg daily and moxifloxacin 400 mg daily, usually for 1 week of total coverage. Fluoroquinolones can be used in patients allergic to penicillin, but should be avoided in pediatric patients because of concern about arthropathy. Another commonly used IV regimen pairs vancomycin (1 gram every 12 hours) for gram-positive coverage with a cephalosporin for gram-negative coverage, such as the third-generation cephalosporin ceftazidime (1 gram every 8 hours). Some studies have also used cefazolin and cefepime.

Definitive treatment comprises globe closure and IOFB extraction, but the optimal timing of extraction remains debated. Immediate extraction means removal during the same operation as globe closure. Compared with delayed extraction, it may lower risks of endophthalmitis and proliferative vitreoretinopathy, although it has not been associated with significant visual improvement. A recent study reported postoperative endophthalmitis in 3.70% after combined globe repair and IOFB removal within 24 hours of injury. In a separate study of 79 eyes injured during Operation Iraqi Freedom and Operation Enduring Freedom, removal occurred an average of 21 days after injury without any endophthalmitis cases. Almost all of these patients (97%) received systemic (86%) and/or topical (85%) antibiotics during the delay. Those findings suggest that delayed extraction with adequate antibiotic coverage may entail minimal endophthalmitis risk in combat-related ocular injury. Every IOFB in that study resulted from exploding ordnance; the authors suggest that heat might sterilize such high-energy projectiles and reduce infection risk. Delay can also permit corneal edema and intraocular inflammation to subside, improving operative visibility, and may allow a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) to form.

Removal timing ultimately depends on physiologic stability, IOFB material, injury characteristics, and access to trained personnel. Endophthalmitis signs indicate immediate surgical extraction unless a simultaneous life-threatening injury contraindicates surgery. Hemodynamic instability justifies postponement. Toxic metals such as iron and copper, and organic foreign bodies, always indicate immediate removal; plastic and glass may remain longer with fewer complications.

document_sections.heading: Surgical management
document_sections.content:
Operative technique must be tailored to IOFB location, dimensions, and composition. The globe should be closed before attempting extraction. For anterior and posterior IOFBs alike, the entry site is identified, and prolapsed tissue is excised or returned to the eye before closure. Corneal lacerations are most commonly closed with 10-0 nylon suture, the limbus with 9-0 nylon suture, and scleral wounds with 8-0 nylon suture. An anterior-segment IOFB is often relatively straightforward to remove: intraocular forceps or magnets can extract it through a separate corneal-limbal incision. Lens involvement may require lensectomy, with intraocular-lens implantation considered later.

For posterior-chamber IOFBs, the principal approach is PPV with extraction during the procedure. PPV also permits treatment of retinal defects, vitreous hemorrhage, and, when necessary, the lens. Standard technique uses three ports and a small-gauge vitrectomy system (23, 25, or 27 gauge). An infusion cannula with a 6-millimeter tip can help when posterior visualization is poor or choroidal hemorrhage is present; anterior-chamber infusion is another option. Core vitrectomy precedes removal of cortical vitreous and, if needed, induction of posterior vitreous detachment. Vitreous may be sampled for Gram stain and culture. Circumferential cutting of vitreous and possible fibrous attachments then frees the IOFB. For an object embedded in retina or choroid, a brief, substantial increase in intraocular pressure may be required to tamponade bleeding as it is dislodged.

If major corneal opacity prevents adequate posterior visualization for PPV, one approach is to work with a cornea specialist to replace the opaque cornea temporarily with a temporary keratoprosthesis (TKP), perform PPV, and complete penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) at the end. Combined vitreoretinal surgery using TKP has, however, been associated with later PKP failure, especially when silicone oil is used. If feasible, waiting for the patient's own cornea to clear may therefore be preferable to immediate keratoplasty. Endoscopic PPV offers another approach, especially for viewing anterior vitreous and pars plana. B-scan ultrasound-guided vitrectomy has also been described when TKP is unsuitable and endoscopy unavailable. An illustrated example shows TKP use during PPV and removal of an IOFB beneath its edge.

An older alternative for posterior-segment extraction uses an external electromagnet to locate and draw the IOFB toward an exit site. The surgeon then incises the overlying sclera, cuts prolapsed vitreous if necessary, and cauterizes choroidal tissue if needed. This method is now uncommon and is not recommended, particularly for posterior-segment IOFBs, because it has been associated with substantial iatrogenic harm. In a cited comparison with PPV, electromagnet extraction produced significantly worse functional and anatomical outcomes and higher rates of endophthalmitis, vitreous hemorrhage, and proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR).

For a large IOFB, typically greater than 4.0 x 4.0 x 4.0 mm, a corneoscleral tunnel is the preferred extraction route. A large pars plana incision can increase retinal incarceration, vitreous hemorrhage, and retinal detachment risks. Smaller objects can be removed through enlarged sclerotomies or pars plana incisions. If the crystalline lens remains present, anterior-chamber extraction is precluded and an enlarged scleral opening is favored.

Intraoperative perfluorocarbon liquid (PFCL) may be injected as a macular shield against a dropped IOFB. Its high specific gravity and surface tension have allowed it to divert falling objects toward peripheral retina. The method remains controversial: some models suggest that an object entering the PFCL could instead descend toward the macula more rapidly. With retinal tears or detachment, care is needed to prevent PFCL from migrating beneath the retina. Another possible macular shield is a small area of coagulated vitreous hemorrhage left in place over the macula; this may be feasible only after delayed extraction, when the blood has had time to coagulate.

After extraction, the surgeon should examine the peripheral retina through 360 degrees with scleral depression. Retinal breaks should be treated thoroughly by laser or cryotherapy; gas or oil tamponade may be placed at the end. Routine prophylactic scleral buckling is debated. Some evidence suggests it may prevent retinal detachment after IOFB removal by PPV. In posterior-segment OGIs, prophylactic buckling has also been associated with better final visual and anatomical outcomes and a non-significant reduction in later retinal detachments.

Intravitreal antibiotics are usually given at completion for endophthalmitis prophylaxis. A frequently used combination is intravitreal vancomycin (1.0 mg/0.1 mL) plus ceftazidime (2.25 mg/0.1 mL) for gram-positive and gram-negative coverage. Where fungal infections are common, the article also describes intravitreal voriconazole (50-100ug/ 0.1mL) or amphotericin B (5-10 ug/0.1mL). Gram stain and culture findings may guide changes in antimicrobial coverage.

document_sections.heading: Instrumentation
document_sections.content:
A small IOFB (<1.0 mm) may be removed with only a vitrector or, if metallic, an intraocular magnet. Intermediate-sized objects (1.0-3.0 mm) may be better suited to intraocular forceps or baskets. Magnet-only extraction is often difficult: an IOFB can detach while traversing sclera or cornea, fall posteriorly, and injure the retina. A magnet can instead transfer the object to forceps or a basket for a firmer grip. Diamond-coated forceps grip through splinters that engage the object's surface and can assist extraction of large IOFBs or smooth ones such as glass.

The NCircle® nitinol tipless stone extractor is an emerging instrument for difficult IOFBs. Originally designed to capture renal calculi in the ureter and kidneys, it uses highly flexible nitinol, a nickel-titanium shape-memory alloy that returns to its original form after deformation and resists kinking. Its basket consists of four nitinol wires controlled by a thumbwheel. The instrument enters the eye with its wires inside a sheath; retracting the sheath near the IOFB opens the basket. After positioning the object inside, advancing the sheath tightens the wires around it, providing a hold unlikely to release during extraction. This is particularly helpful for objects that are irregular, round, large, or smooth, including glass. Forceps, or magnets for ferromagnetic IOFBs, can help position an object in the basket. The device's reach is sufficient for the posterior pole even in eyes with the most extreme axial lengths.

document_sections.heading: Published outcomes
document_sections.content:
At least 21% of eyes with IOFBs have final visual acuity worse than 20/200. The Ocular Trauma Score can reliably predict final vision in the injured eye. Factors associated with poor visual prognosis include age greater than 50, worse presenting visual acuity, hyphema, vitreous hemorrhage, uveal prolapse, retinal detachment, afferent pupillary defect, retinal hemorrhage, complications of retinal breaks, and intraocular perfluoropropane (C3F8) gas tamponade. Central corneal perforation, corneoscleral laceration, larger IOFBs, and posterior-segment IOFBs are likewise associated with worse visual outcomes. IOFBs have also been associated with higher postoperative rates of proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) and phthisis bulbi. Factors linked to better visual outcomes include better initial visual acuity, no retinal breaks, no vitreous hemorrhage, a wound length less than 4 mm, and non-vitrectomy surgery.

Patients with previous IOFBs should receive counseling about eye protection during exposure to chemicals, lasers, metal, UV equipment, and other high-risk activities. For poor visual outcomes, clinicians should devote substantial time to explaining monocular precautions, including 3 mm polycarbonate lenses and safety frames worn at all times. Low-vision referral can help patients make the most of remaining sight and adjust to their changed visual baseline.

Mental-health consequences of the injury should also be assessed. Traumatic OGIs have been associated with a high prevalence of anxiety and depression in adults and children. In a small pediatric cohort, 15% developed generalized anxiety disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, and depression after ocular trauma. Attention to this possibility during postoperative visits can help identify patients who may benefit from mental-health referral. Assessment and treatment of mental-health disorders related to the traumatic IOFB experience are important.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The review brings together evidence on IOFB characteristics, incidence, preoperative care, and operative approaches. Because over half of IOFB injuries occur at work, the authors emphasize encouraging eye protection whenever risk is present. Suspected IOFB calls for a thorough but gentle examination using slit-lamp biomicroscopy and indirect ophthalmoscopy to locate the object and associated damage. Noncontrast orbital CT is the first-line imaging study for localization and operative planning. Extraction may take place immediately or after a delay once globe closure has been achieved; patient health, visibility for prompt removal, and the care setting inform that choice. Operative timing and technique depend heavily on clinical circumstances, while PPV remains the main approach for posterior-segment IOFBs. The NCircle ® nitinol stone basket is identified as an emerging aid for objects that are difficult to grasp. Further research is needed on acute and chronic IOFB complications, factors favoring better visual outcomes, and optimal surgical approaches; improved understanding could strengthen identification and treatment of patients with IOFB-related ocular injury.
